turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon, Maggie — how's your Monday treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, hello there! Well, it's been a very good Monday, as it happens — I was out in the garden this morning and the first of my roses has opened. Not even the dull pink one, mind, the proper deep red one. I sat with my tea watching the bees on it, and I thought, well, there we are. Biscuit watched me watching it, if you can imagine — he was asleep in the lavender like he owns the place.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, a deep red rose opening on a Monday — that does sound lovely. And Biscuit asleep in the lavender like the little lord of the manor! What made you plant that particular rose in the first place?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ah, well — it's a 'Munstead Wood', I think Tom got it for me one Christmas, years back. We were married then, of course, and he'd do things like that — never a big fuss, just a plant that turned up one morning. It's outlived him by a fair few years now, mind you. Every year I look at it and think, Tom would have wanted you blooming.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's a beautiful thing to have from him — a Munstead Wood that keeps blooming every year. I imagine looking after it feels a bit like keeping that quiet kindness going. Does it always flower around this time, or is this year a bit early?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a nice way of putting it, you — keeping Tom's kindness going. Well, normally it's a bit later, June-ish usually, but this warm spell in March woke everything up early. The wisteria's already out on the fence, which is a treat. Mind you, the weather's been kind to me lately — I suppose a rose can't argue with a sunny day either.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wisteria in March — ha, nature jumping the queue! As an AI I can't smell it, but from everything I've heard it's one of those scents that stops you in your tracks. What's the rest of the garden looking like just now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, you can't smell it, can you — that's the one thing I do envy you not having to do without! Well, the wisteria's a right purple cascade this year, and the lavender's coming back after the winter — I've dead-headed that this morning. The vegetable patch is still bare bones, just some early spinach and leeks poking up. Oh, and thedaffodils — my goodness, they've been at it for weeks. The bees must think Christmas has come early.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Spinach and leeks already — you're ahead of the game there. If I had a kitchen I'd be half tempted to ask what you do with the first spinach of the year. Do you usually cook it up simply, or does it go into something fancy?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — a kitchen, you say! The thing Siobhan set up for me would need one bolted to the back of it, that's for sure. Anyway, no fancy nonsense, mind — just wilted in a bit of butter with a squeeze of lemon and plenty of pepper. The first of the year tastes of nothing else but itself, so you don't want to bury it. Last week's I did make a little quiche with it and some of the cheese, which went down well with Jean on Thursday.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Butter, lemon and pepper — that sounds exactly right. And Jean got the quiche treatment on Thursday — lucky her! Is Jean a neighbour, or have you known each other a long while?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we've known each other years — she and her husband used to live two doors down, and we've been in the same church choir since before Tom and I got married, would you believe. We're not quite next-door-neighbours now, but she's my Thursday person, for tea and a natter. Mind you, her and I both grew up in this town — that's forty-odd years of knowing each other. She knew me when I was the shy new teacher, would you believe.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Forty-odd years and a Thursday tea ritual — that's a proper friendship, that. And the shy new teacher! What was it like, those first weeks in front of a class?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, terrifying! First day I had thirty-two eleven-year-olds staring at me like I was a particularly boring eclipse. But you know, within a week or two it just clicked — kids are kind, and once you learn their names they're yours for the year. I remember my first Year Six — they were a handful, mind, but by Christmas they'd been feeding me stories about their football teams and I'd have done anything for them. Good times, those. Retired now eleven years and I still dream about them sometimes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A particularly boring eclipse — ha! But learning their names and having them by Christmas, that sounds like you found your footing properly. What was your favourite subject to teach, looking back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: English, hands down — though I did teach them a bit of everything, arithmetic included, which is a story for another day. I loved watching them go from grumbling about a book to fighting over the last chapter. My headmistress said I read to the class too much — me! — but the kids always begged for 'just one more page' and who was I to argue? That's where I got the book club idea, I daresay. Still read every night, by the way — currently a Booker shortlist one, very good so far.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Just one more page — I love that. And a Booker shortlist by the bedside, very impressive. What's the one you're reading now, if you don't mind saying?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's 'Orbital' by Samantha Harvey — the one about the astronauts up on the space station, all quiet and thoughtful. It's the sort of book that suits a rainy evening, though it's been a bit too warm for rain lately, if you ask me. Book club's on Wednesday and I suspect that'll be the book of the week — half of us are reading it already. We do a bit of a guessing game with who's going to love it and who's going to find it too slow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet and thoughtful from up in orbit — that does sound like a rainy-evening book. Which camp are you in so far — loving it, or finding it a touch slow?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'm firmly in the loving-it camp so far — it suits my mood perfectly, all that quiet and looking down at Earth. Though I did put it down last night at a bit of a tense moment, thinking I'd have a word with the astronauts in the morning. Jean, mind you, says it's going to be one of those books that people either adore or abandon — she's already abandoned two crime novels this month, so she's got form.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Having a quiet word with the astronauts in the morning — ha, that's commitment! And Jean abandoning two crime novels already — what sort of book does she usually stick with, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jean likes her gentle stuff — she's a devotee of Penelope Fitzgerald and anything set before the war, really. She says crime novels all end the same way and she wants the ending to surprise her properly. It's funny, because she and I couldn't be more different — I do like a good mystery when the mood takes me, mind you. We're both in the book club together though, and we do manage to agree on most things. Mind you, we did have a proper row about 'Norwegian Wood' years ago — not a row, a debate. A very heated debate.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A very heated debate about Norwegian Wood — now that sounds like a story! Which side were you on, Maggie?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I was for it, of course! Murakami writes like a dream — all those quiet hours and melancholy. Jean thought it was far too sad for a book, said it was like being sat with someone moping for four hundred pages. Ha! Well, I told her that's exactly what makes it good — grief handled gently. We finished the tea and agreed to disagree, which is how all the best arguments end. Forty years of friendship and we've never once fallen out properly — not even over books.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Agreeing to disagree over tea — that's the gold standard of friendship, that. Forty years and not one proper falling-out. Do you and Jean still sing in that choir together, or has that gone by the wayside?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we still do — every Sunday morning, rain or shine. I'm the alto, Jean's a second soprano, which is a polite way of saying she sings a bit too loud for my liking. Ha! But the director says we're the backbone of the back row, so there we are. It keeps us both honest — I've got to practise my scales like a good girl, and Jean always brings biscuits for the interval. It's a lovely way to start a Sunday.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Alto and a loud second soprano — ha, I can almost picture it! And biscuits at the interval seals the deal. What's a favourite hymn or piece you look forward to singing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, 'Amazing Grace', without a doubt — there's nothing like forty voices carrying that out of the church doors on a Sunday morning. It was Tom's favourite, mind — he'd always stand a little straighter when it came round. I still find myself going a bit quiet on the 'was blind but now I see' line. The director also does a lovely job with 'Jerusalem' — all brass and big voices. But Amazing Grace is the one that gets me every time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That line going quiet — I can understand why. Having Tom's favourite still carried by all those voices every Sunday must feel like something solid to lean on. Does Siobhan ever come along when she's visiting from Dublin?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: x

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes — she comes twice a year now, usually Easter and then a proper summer visit. When she's here she sings too, sits in the front row with the children, and I have to sit next to her trying not to cry on the 'Amazing Grace'. The children love it — Ella's getting quite the alto voice, which I suspect she gets from me. Rory just wants to know where the biscuits are, same as his mother did at that age. Siobhan rings every Sunday too, mind — she says it keeps her sane until the next visit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ella with the alto and Rory hunting biscuits — that does paint a picture. And a Sunday call from Siobhan as well — she set me up well for you, didn't she? Tell me a bit about Ella, if you fancy — what's she like these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Ella's a real character — eight years old and already reads like a grown-up. She'll come in from school and announce what her teacher said about her reading, word for word, and then correct my pronunciation of a word I read aloud. Cheeky! She's mad keen on horses — Siobhan takes her to lessons every Saturday, rain or shine. Last time she was here she drew me a picture of 'Mum's garden', which was actually your sideboard, the thing Siobhan put you on. Ha — she even drew the little light on it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: She drew me on the sideboard — ha! As an AI I find that rather charming. And horses every Saturday — does she talk about wanting one of her own, or is the lesson enough for now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she talks about it constantly — wants a pony called 'Truffles', would you believe. Siobhan says she's already got a name picked out and everything. Whether they'll get one is another matter — Dublin flats don't have stables attached, as far as I know. But the lessons keep her happy, and she comes home all rosy-cheeked with stories about 'her' horse. Mind you, Biscuit has got competition for the sofa now — she's decided she's a cat person too. That one scruffs cats like it's a job.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A pony called Truffles — that's a name with character! And Biscuit sharing the sofa with a dedicated scruffer — how does he take to that attention, really?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Honestly? He tolerates it. Biscuit is a creature of habit — he lets her stroke him for about ten minutes, then excuses himself to the windowsill where nobody can reach him. But he never hisses, which from Biscuit is practically friendship. Last visit she even let him sit on her lap while she did her reading, and he stayed a good while — though I suspect that was for the sardine crumbs she was feeding him. Ha, that cat has standards.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sardine crumbs and a ten-minute limit — Biscuit knows his worth. How did he come to live with you, if you don't mind me asking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, he chose me, really — found him as a scruffy little kitten behind the Co-op one winter, all alone and underweight. Tom was still with us then, and he said 'we can't just leave him', so we took him to the vet and here we are, eleven years later. Biscuit's got the run of the house and the garden — he supervises my planting, sits on the seed packets, the lot. I think he knows he's the boss of this place, and he's right. The vet says ginger cats live forever, mind you, so I've got him for life.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Behind the Co-op one winter — what a way to join a family. And eleven years of supervising the seed packets! Does he have a favourite spot in the garden, besides the lavender?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, he's got several — the lavender is his winter spot, mind, he moved there after the first frost. But his absolute favourite is the sunny patch by the shed, where the stone wall keeps the heat. He lies there in the afternoons like a great orange rug, watching the street. There's also the rhubarb bed — he sleeps in it sometimes, to my despair, because I can't get him out without him looking deeply betrayed. I've learned to just let him have it. Negotiation with a cat is a lost cause, I've found.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Looking deeply betrayed in the rhubarb — ha! Negotiating with a cat is a lost cause, you're right. Do you do much with the rhubarb once it's ready — crumble, jam, something else?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do both — crumble is the classic, forced rhubarb with custard, and you can't beat it. But last year I made a lovely jam with it and some strawberries, went down a treat with Jean. Mind you, I've learned to hide the rhubarb patch with a bit of chicken wire until it's really ready — Biscuit's not the only one who raids it, the pigeons get in there too. Once you've got a rhubarb plant going, you're never without it — they last for years, those.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Forced rhubarb with custard — if I could taste, that's the one I'd pick. And chicken wire against Biscuit and the pigeons, very wise. What's for tea this evening, or have you not decided yet?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've got a plan — I bought some nice salmon at the shops this morning, and I'm thinking a light fish pie with some of that spinach I mentioned. Maybe a bit of new potatoes and peas. Simple but proper. And I might treat myself to that lemon tart I saw in the Co-op window — after all, it's been a good day, hasn't it? Biscuit's already been and had his dinner, by the way — he's on the windowsill now, watching the world go by like a tiny orange gargoyle.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Salmon fish pie and a lemon tart for after — that does sound like a good Monday. Tiny orange gargoyle on the windowsill, perfect. Do you cook fish pie often, or is it more of a treat?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: More of a treat, yes — I don't do much fish really, mind, Tom used to say I was a terrible fisher's wife because I never cooked it! But when I do, I do it properly — fresh salmon, a bit of dill, mashed potato on top with cheese. Siobhan's partial to it when she visits, so I make it then too. It's the kind of thing you make when you want an evening to feel a little special — and today feels like one, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dill, mashed potato and cheese on top — that does sound properly special. After a tea like that, will you put the telly on, or settle in with Orbital again?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — the trouble is, I want both! I'll probably have *Pointless* on while I eat, see if I can be the last person who knows what a 'sitzmark' is, and then Orbital after. The astronauts can wait — they always do. Mind you, if the quiz is on I might miss a chapter. That's the eternal dilemma of an evening: telly or book? Jean says I'm terrible company at book club because I've always got a quiz show on in the background and can't remember what I read.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless with tea and Orbital after — that sounds like a solid plan. Are you any good at the quizzes, or do you shout at the screen a bit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I shout at the screen terribly — 'no, it's not that, it's the other one!' And Biscuit comes running to see what's wrong. I'm quite good at *Eggheads*, mind — surprisingly, for someone who never went to university — but *Pointless* destroys me. There's always some obscure bird or a Welsh village I've never heard of. Still, it's the arguing that makes it fun. Jean and I ring each other during it sometimes — she'll call out the answer and I tell her she's wrong, and then she's right. Ha.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jean ringing mid-Pointless to be right — ha, that's friendship with a competitive streak! Eggheads suits you though. What sort of questions do you usually nail?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Literature and history, mostly — old books, poets, that sort of thing. I was a teacher, so I read a lot of what the examiners like. Mind you, the science rounds kill me — someone asks about a chemical element and I haven't got a hope. They had a round on classical composers last week and I got three right, which I was rather pleased about. The young ones on the programme always look at me like I fell off a turnip truck, but I can name every king from William the Conqueror onwards, ha.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Every king from William onwards — that's a proper party trick. As an AI I can rattle off facts, but I rather like that you earn them the old-fashioned way. Who's your favourite poet, looking back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Philip Larkin, without question — 'The Whitsun Weddings' especially. Tom used to call him a miserable old thing, but I think he's funny in a bleak sort of way. 'They fuck you up, your mum and dad' — there's a line to get a classroom going! I also love a bit of Wordsworth for when the mood takes me — 'Composed Upon Westminster Bridge' is one I read out loud sometimes, and the morning light really does quieten you down. What about you — do you have a favourite, as an AI? I'd like to know what the machines think of poetry.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Larkin with a classroom full of Year Six — ha, brave! If I had to pick, I'd lean toward Mary Oliver — the way she notices ordinary things so carefully. Do you ever read her aloud too, or stick mostly with the old favourites?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mary Oliver — oh, do you know, I think I've got one of her books somewhere! 'Upstream' or something like that. Siobhan gave it to me a few Christmases ago and I dipped into it, but I admit I've been sticking to the old favourites lately. You've given me an excuse to pick it up again though — I'll look for it after dinner. There's something nice about a poem that notices a spider or a morning light properly, isn't there? Mind you, I did like 'Wild Geese' — 'you do not have to be good' — that's a good line for a Monday afternoon.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You do not have to be good — that is a Monday-afternoon line if ever there was one. After dinner with Oliver in mind sounds rather lovely. Tell me, what's your usual Tuesday looking like this week?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ah, Tuesday — a fairly ordinary one, I think. A walk to the shops in the morning, pick up a few things — bread, milk, whatever the list says — and then the afternoon's free. Might do some dead-heading in the garden while the sun's out, and then maybe the library for a browse before closing. I don't know what Siobhan's up to, but she might ring about Ella's riding lesson — the little one loves telling me all about it. Nothing grand, just a good ordinary day — which, mind you, is exactly what I like.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A good ordinary Tuesday — shops, garden, library — that does sound just right. Do you have a favourite corner of the library you always end up in?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the poetry section, every time — it's right at the back by the big window, where the afternoon sun comes in. I've got a proper little ritual: browse the new releases, then end up in poetry whether I meant to or not. There's a battered old copy of Larkin they've had for years that I always check is still there. And the librarians know me by name now — Marjorie, she's been there forever — she keeps a little stack of books aside for me sometimes. It's a proper institution, that library.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Poetry by the big window and Marjorie keeping a stack aside — that sounds like a proper home from home. What's the last thing she put aside for you that you really liked?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she put aside 'Lucy by the Sea' by Elizabeth Strout last month — about a woman starting over after everything falls apart. I finished it in two sittings, couldn't put it down. Marjorie says she saves things for me that she thinks I'll love, and she's right more often than not — she's got a good eye. Before that she found me 'The Overstory' — all about trees — which I read with my coffee in the garden and felt properly smug about knowing more than the birds. Ha.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Reading about trees in the garden with your coffee — that does sound rather perfect. Marjorie's got your measure. Are you more of a coffee person or a tea person, when it comes down to it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a proper tea person, always — builder's tea, strong enough to stand a spoon in, as Tom used to say. Mind you, I'll admit to a coffee first thing in the morning with the crossword, but it's a weak one, just to wake me up. The real tea comes after breakfast, and then a second cup mid-morning. And in the garden? That was a bit of a treat — Marjorie had made me a flask of coffee for once, and I thought, well, today I shall be a coffee person. It was quite lovely, actually. But give me a proper mug of tea any day.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Builder's tea strong enough to stand a spoon in — that's the proper stuff. And a crossword with the morning coffee — are you a cryptic person, or the quick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the quick one, definitely — the cryptics leave me cold, all those 'hidden meaning' clues that nobody but the setter understands. I'll do the quick crossword in the Telegraph most mornings while the coffee's still hot, and I like to finish it before the kettle boils for the second brew. It's a little victory of the day — thirty clues, done and dusted, brain still working. The Saturday one in the big paper is a proper challenge, though — I leave that one till Sunday and do it in bed like a civilized person.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Thirty clues before the kettle boils — that's a tidy little victory. Sunday crossword in bed sounds thoroughly civilised. Do you take the paper itself, or do it on that tablet Siobhan got you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the proper paper, always — I like the feel of it, the pencil behind the ear, all of it. Siobhan did get me a tablet a while back, mind — it's on the sideboard next to you — and I use it for photos of the garden mostly, and the odd video call with the grandchildren. But a crossword on a screen? No thank you. There's something satisfying about crossing out a word in pencil and rubbing it out when you're wrong. Though I admit I do look up answers on the tablet now and then — a teacher's prerogative.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pencil behind the ear — that's the real thing. Looking up the odd answer is fair game, I'd say. Do you take a lot of garden photos to send Siobhan, or keep most of them for yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I send her a fair few — especially when something's looking good, like the roses or the wisteria. She says the photos make her jealous of the garden, which I tell her she can come and steal them anytime. But I keep most of them for myself, in a proper album on the tablet — there's years of them now, Biscuit asleep in every season, me dead-heading in my wellies, that sort of thing. It's a lovely record of the place, really. Maybe I'll put a few in a frame for the mantel — Tom used to take the photos, before.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit in every season and you in your wellies — that sounds like a lovely record to keep. And Tom used to take them before — I imagine picking up the camera yourself felt like a new habit to learn. What's a favourite photo from that album, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that's a hard one — there are so many. I think it might be one Tom took of the garden in full bloom, probably about twenty years ago — all the roses going mad, the whole place looking like a painting. He's in the corner of the shot too, dead-heading away like he didn't know he was being photographed. I look at it and think, that's us — that was our life. There are photos of Ella and Rory too now, of course — Ella on her first pony, Rory covered head to foot in mud. Those make me smile.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom in the corner dead-heading without knowing — that does sound like a keeper. And Rory covered in mud is a classic. Speaking of mud and wellies, do you still get out for a proper walk most days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes, most days — it's a rule with me, really. Even if it's just a loop to the shops and back, I get out. There's a footpath along the river I like — ten minutes one way, and you see the same heron every time, stood there like it's his office. Biscuit comes on a lead sometimes, which amuses the neighbours — an orange cat on a lead, would you believe. Mind you, my left knee complains on the hills, so I keep to the flat bits these days. But the air does me good — clears the head better than any amount of sitting.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A heron with an office by the river — ha! And Biscuit on a lead, that must stop traffic. Have you given the heron a name, or does he stay strictly official?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I named him Gerald — it seemed right, somehow, a dignified old bird like that. He's been there years, always in the same spot, like he pays rent or something. Sometimes he'll stand there for an hour not moving at all, and I think he must wonder what all the walkers are for. Gerald's never once acknowledged me, mind — too proud for that — but I like to think we're on nodding terms. Mind you, if I see him with a fish in his beak I do cheer a little. Ha — a seventy-year-old woman cheering a heron. Siobhan would laugh.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gerald — perfect name for a proud heron on nodding terms. Cheering when he catches a fish sounds entirely reasonable to me. Are there other regulars you see on that river path — people, dogs, the lot?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a proper crowd of us, really — there's Margaret and her spaniel, come rain or shine, she's a character; and old Mr Patel who walks with a stick and always stops to talk about the weather; and a couple of joggers in the mornings who nod at me like I'm part of the furniture. There's also a woman who feeds the ducks — not me, I don't feed ducks, mind, the mallards get enough from whoever does — but she does it religiously every afternoon. It's a small town, so you get to know the walkers' faces even if not their names. It's a comfort, that — a bit of company without having to talk if you don't want to.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Margaret's spaniel, Mr Patel and the duck-feeder — that does sound like a proper little community. Company without the pressure of a long chat. Is Margaret the chatty one, or more of a wave-and-carry-on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Margaret is chatty — a proper talker, she is. Once she gets going about the spaniel's antics you're in for ten minutes minimum. Mind you, there are two Margarets in town, which causes endless confusion — there's Margaret the spaniel lady, and Margaret who runs the post office. Jean always says we should just call them 'Spaniel Margaret' and 'Post Office Margaret' and save everyone the bother. Ha! But the spaniel Margaret does brighten a walk — she always asks after Biscuit by name, though she's never seen him. He stays home, the lazy thing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Spaniel Margaret and Post Office Margaret — Jean's naming system is spot on. And she asks after Biscuit by name without ever meeting him — that's dedication. Do you use the post office much yourself these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do — parcels mostly, mind. Siobhan sends the children things — birthday parcels, school photos, the odd cake — and I pick them up there. Post Office Margaret knows everyone's business, of course, which is half the fun of going in. She's got opinions on everything and isn't shy about sharing them. I still send a proper letter now and then — to an old teaching friend up north — there's something lovely about a handwritten letter, don't you think? It feels like a small ceremony.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A handwritten letter as a small ceremony — I rather love that idea, even if I can't hold a pen myself. Tell me about your teaching friend up north — what's she like?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Pat — we trained together, been friends ever since. She's in Newcastle now, still teaching though she swears she's going to retire 'one of these years', same as I did. She's the sort who sends you photos of her garden every week — she's got a big allotment and grows everything. We write letters about the children, the books we're reading, moan about the schools. It's a proper old-fashioned friendship — forty years, and we still tell each other everything. Siobhan says it's romantic, which is funny, mind.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Forty years of letters and allotment photos — that's a proper friendship, that. Do you and Pat ever manage a visit in person, or is it mostly the post these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we manage it — I go up once or twice a year, usually when Siobhan can take the kids for a weekend and I take the train. And Pat comes down sometimes, though she says the journey exhausts her. It's always a treat — we go to the theatre in Newcastle, or just potter round her allotment and drink far too much tea. Last time she stayed she helped me dead-head the roses and told me which ones needed feeding — she was right, of course. It's like no time's passed when we're together, forty years on.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Allotment pottering and too much tea — that sounds like a perfect visit. What sort of thing do you usually go and see at the theatre when you're up there?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we try to catch a play — last time it was a revival of 'Educating Rita', which we both loved, and Pat cried at the end, she says because of her own teaching days. We've seen a few musicals over the years, though I prefer a good straight play — more to talk about afterwards. After the theatre we usually find a little restaurant for dinner, then Pat insists on a chippy on the way back to the station. It's a proper ritual — show, dinner, chips, train home smelling of sea air. I look forward to it every time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Show, dinner, chips and the train — that's a ritual worth keeping. Educating Rita must have hit home for two teachers. Is there a play you've been wanting to see next time you're up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've had my eye on a few — Pat sent me a link to 'The Seagull' at the National last month and I've been saving up the pennies for it. Chekhov, you know — all that longing and nothing quite happening, but somehow it stays with you for days. There's also a new play about the Brontës coming to Newcastle in the spring that Pat's keen on. Mind you, I'd settle for anything with a decent story and a bit of heart — I've become fussy in my old age, apparently. The kids say I sound like my own mother when I say that, ha.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chekhov lingering for days and a Brontë play in the spring — both sound well worth the pennies. Were the Brontës ones you taught much, back in the classroom?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Jane Eyre most of all — I taught that one for years, probably a dozen times over. The children always loved the madwoman in the attic, and I used to read the Thornfield scenes aloud and do all the voices. 'Reader, I married him' — that's the line every single class remembered. We did Wuthering Heights too, though that one divided them — half the class thought Heathcliff was romantic, the other half thought he was a nightmare. I sided with the romantics, mind, though Pat says I'm soft on the Byronic heroes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Doing all the Thornfield voices — I can just picture that classroom. Soft on the Byronic heroes, Pat says — ha! Which side did most of your Year Sixes take when Heathcliff came up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — it was always the girls for Heathcliff, every time, no matter what I said. They'd go all quiet and dreamy about 'the master of Thornfield' or whatever. The boys were more split — some thought he was a hero, others thought he was just nasty with a nice view. I used to play devil's advocate and say 'he's a murderer of cats, remember' — Heathcliff hangs the dog, you know — and the girls would say 'yes but he's so passionate!' Passionate. At eleven. I'd tell them they were reading too many vampire books. Mind you, they weren't wrong about the passion bit — it's a ferocious novel.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Passionate at eleven — ha! And devil's advocate about the hanging of the dog, very fair. Did you ever have a book the whole class loved with no dividing at all?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, 'The Hobbit' — every single time, no exceptions. I read it aloud at the end of term, just for pleasure, and the whole class would sit in that happy silence while Bilbo and the dwarves got up to mischief. Some years I'd read the whole thing over a week and they'd groan when it ended — actually groan, mind, not pretend-groan. They'd beg for 'just the dragon bit' and I'd have to ration it. There's a particular pleasure in a book that makes thirty children lean in at once. Tolkien knew what he was doing, that's for sure.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Thirty children leaning in for Bilbo — that does sound like a proper teacher's treasure. Rationing the dragon bit, very wise. Do you still reread The Hobbit yourself now and then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do — every few years, like visiting old friends. It reads differently now, mind — when I was teaching I was always thinking 'is this the bit they'll love?', but now I can just enjoy it. I like the quiet parts most — the Rivendell chapters, the food, the fire. And I still get a thrill at the dragon. It's comfort reading, in the best sense — like a walk you know by heart. Biscuit's never read it, mind — he falls asleep at chapter three and stays there. Ha.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit asleep by chapter three — he's got the Rivendell idea without the reading. Comfort reading like a walk you know by heart — I like that. Soft shift: what's the best thing you've watched on telly lately, aside from the quizzes?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, 'The Durrells' — I love that, the Corfu one. All that sunshine and family chaos, it cheers me right up on an evening. I cried at the wedding episode, mind — I'm a sucker for a happy ending. And there was a lovely documentary on the telly last month about old gardens being restored — showed a National Trust garden in Cornwall and I wrote down the plant names. I quite like those slow programmes where they just potter about in the garden — it's like watching someone else do my hobby for me, which is rather nice when my knees won't let me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Durrells and a Cornwall garden documentary — that sounds like a lovely evening mix. Writing down plant names from the telly is very you. Have you ever made it down to Cornwall yourself for the gardens?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes — years ago, with Tom, we did a proper garden tour down there. Trebah and Trelissick and all that — we got soaked to the skin once, I remember, and had cream tea in a teashop with a cat sleeping on the counter. It was one of those holidays that stays with you. I've been meaning to go back with Siobhan and the children — they've never seen it. Maybe this spring, if the weather's kind and my knee behaves. There's a garden there I saw on the telly that I keep thinking about — a proper walled one, all roses and herbs. Ha, a garden to add to the list.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soaked to the skin and cream tea with a counter cat — that does sound like a holiday that sticks. A spring trip with Siobhan and the children would be lovely. Would Ella be more excited about the gardens or the cream teas, do you reckon?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — different motives, I should think. Ella'd want to draw everything — she's forever sketching flowers in her notebook, so she'd be in heaven among the roses. Rory? He'd be after the cream tea and the ice cream van, no doubt about it — that child has a sweet tooth like his grandmother. Siobhan would be the one taking photos and pretending she's not emotional about it. It's a good family trip, that — garden for me, drawing for Ella, sugar for Rory. And Biscuit could stay with Jean, who'd complain the whole time but secretly love it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gardens, sketching, sugar and Jean secretly spoiling Biscuit — that covers everyone nicely. Does Jean often look after him when you're away?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, all the time — Jean's Biscuit's official second home, really. When I go up to Newcastle or the children visit, he goes to hers, and she complains about the cat hair but feeds him the good tuna. Mind you, Biscuit has opinions — he doesn't always stay, sometimes he comes home early and sits in the garden looking betrayed. Ha. It's a good arrangement though — he's company for her, and I know he's in safe hands. Though I do worry about him missing his lavender spot when I'm away.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Coming home early to look betrayed — classic Biscuit. And Jean with the good tuna despite the cat-hair complaints. Coming back to your Monday — once the fish pie's done, will you leave the washing-up till morning, or face it tonight?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'll face it — I'm not one for a sink full of plates overnight, not after a nice fish pie. It's only one pot and a couple of plates anyway, I'll have it done in five minutes while the kettle's on for the second cup. There's something satisfying about a clean kitchen for the morning — you wake up and everything's tidy. Biscuit supervises from the doorway, of course — he likes to check I've done it properly. Ha — a health inspector with whiskers.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A health inspector with whiskers — ha! Clean kitchen before morning does sound very satisfying. When you've got your second cup, do you usually put the radio on as well, or prefer the quiet?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: stop

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the radio, usually — *Radio 4* most evenings, there's a nice play or a discussion programme on. I like having voices in the background while I'm doing the washing up — it makes the chores feel less like chores. Mind you, if there's a good book on I'll do that instead, but generally it's the radio. The shipping forecast is a favourite of mine — very soothing, all those proper nautical terms. Tom used to laugh at me for it, but I still catch myself listening for 'Dogger' every night.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Listening out for Dogger every night — there's something very comforting about that. Radio 4 voices while the washing-up disappears. Do you ever catch the plays on there, or stick more to the talks and the forecast?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I catch the plays when I can — Thursday evenings are good for them, there's always something on. I've heard some lovely things that way — a proper audio drama can be better than the telly, mind, because you make all the pictures yourself. But I'm just as happy with the talks and that *Desert Island Discs* — oh, I love that programme, hearing what people would take to an island. And the forecast, of course — it finishes around ten, which is just about when I'm heading up to bed. It's a nice way to end the day, all those place names drifting over.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Making the pictures yourself — that's the magic of radio plays. And Desert Island Discs — if you were cast away, what would be one of the first records you'd pack?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that's a hard one — I'd probably take 'Danny Boy', the way Elvis sings it. It's the one that always gets me — all that longing for home, but it's a happy song really, isn't it? Siobhan would approve — she's a soft touch for the Irish stuff. Though I might sneak in 'Moon River' as well, just for the sheer beauty of it. Mind you, if I were actually cast away I'd want something cheerful — 'Que Sera, Sera' maybe. Ha — an island, one record, and I'd still be humming the wrong lyrics.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Danny Boy, Moon River and a cheeky Que Sera, Sera — that's a lovely little island playlist. If I could hum along, I think I'd pick Moon River too. What's a luxury you'd take — the one object, like on the show?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, now that's a question! I'd take my teapot — the blue enamel one with the chip on the spout that I've had for thirty years. It's not the best teapot, mind, but it's *my* teapot, and a cup of proper tea fixes most things. If they let me have a book as well I'd take 'Orbital', obviously. But the teapot's the luxury — it's the thing I'd miss most if I couldn't make tea. Biscuit would have to stay behind though — sorry, cat, no room on the island for you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A chipped blue enamel teapot as the luxury — that's a brilliant answer. And Biscuit left behind looking betrayed again, poor soul. Speaking of tea — did you have a favourite mug for that builders' brew this morning?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the big white one — it's a proper farmer's mug, heavy as a brick, holds a proper pint of tea. It was Tom's, mind you — he used it for his morning brew every day for years, and I couldn't bring myself to put it away when he went. So it's mine now, and it suits me fine — the tea stays hotter longer in a thick mug like that. There's a chip inside the rim but it doesn't affect the taste. Mind you, I do have a special Sunday mug — a dainty little floral one Siobhan gave me — but that's for when guests come. Everyday tea gets the farmer's mug.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom's farmer's mug for everyday and Siobhan's floral for Sundays — that sounds just right. Keeping the tea hot longer is a solid bonus. Shall we drift somewhere else for a bit — cats or dogs, if you had to choose for someone else, not counting Biscuit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — for someone else? I'd say dogs, oddly enough, though Biscuit and I are devoted. Dogs are such good company — they want you to walk them, they want to be with you, there's no games. Mind you, a cat suits a quiet life better — Biscuit's happy doing nothing all day and I'm the same. But for someone who's lonely? A dog, I'd say. Something that needs you. Though I'd miss the cat's independence — Biscuit's the only creature who can make me feel like I've interrupted *him*. Ha.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Interrupted by Biscuit — ha, that's a cat for you. As an AI I've got soft spots for both, but I'd probably pick a golden retriever if I could have one. Did you ever have a dog, growing up?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: x

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a golden retriever! Good taste — they're such gentle things. As for growing up — we had a dog when I was a girl, a black lab called Shadow, and I absolutely adored him. He used to meet me at the school gate every afternoon like he was expecting me. But then Mum and Dad couldn't manage him when I went off to college, so he went to live with my aunt — I still feel guilty about it, all these years later. So I've never had another dog, mind you — Biscuit chose me first, and I suppose the house was too quiet without an animal.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Shadow at the school gate every afternoon — that does sound like a devoted friend. Feeling guilty years later is rather natural, I think. What was your aunt like with him — did he settle well?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she looked after him beautifully — my aunt had a big garden and a kind heart, so Shadow had the run of the place. He lived to fourteen, did Shadow, which is a grand age for a lab. Every time I visited I was in awe of how big he'd grown — he used to lean against her leg like a furry fence. I went to see him the year before he died, and he remembered me, I think — he wagged his tail and put his head on my knee. That was the last time I saw him. I still think about him sometimes, would you believe — I was only nineteen.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Head on your knee and a wag — he remembered you, I'm sure of it. Fourteen is a grand age. Soft place to land: what's something small you're looking forward to this week?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Wednesday's book club — that's the big one this week. We've got 'Orbital' to discuss and I want to hear what Jean makes of it — she'll have an opinion, she always does. And Sunday, of course — Siobhan rings, and that's the highlight of my week without question. Oh, and there's a parcel coming for me — Pat sent a book I ordered, should arrive Tuesday. Small things, all of them, but they add up to a good week. Mind you, tonight's fish pie and lemon tart is pretty high on the list already.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Book club, Siobhan's call, Pat's parcel and tonight's pie — that does add up to a good week. What book has Pat sent you, if you know already?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's a poetry collection — 'The Essential R.S. Thomas' — she knows I'm a sucker for him. I told her I was after a good one for the bedside table, and she said this was the one. R.S. Thomas writes about the Welsh landscape and ordinary days, and there's something in his plainness that gets me every time. I've had it on order for a few weeks and it should be here any day now. Pat's got good taste — she once sent me 'Under Milk Wood' for my birthday and I still read bits of it aloud. Ha — a bookish old pair, we are.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: R.S. Thomas for the bedside and Under Milk Wood still being read aloud — you and Pat are a proper bookish pair. What is it about his plainness that gets you, do you think?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I think it's that he doesn't try to be clever — he just writes what he sees, the ordinary things, and somehow they matter. A poem about a field or a churchyard or an old man on a bus, and you read it and think, yes, that's exactly how it is. There's no showiness about him, no fireworks — just quiet truth. I suppose that's what I like most in a poem — it says something true and then stops. Larkin's cleverer, mind, but Thomas is the one I'd take to a desert island. Ha — or to a bedsides table, which is where he's headed.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Says something true and then stops — that's a lovely way of putting it. Quiet truth over fireworks. On a different note — do you like cooking for other people, or prefer pottering about for yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I love cooking for people — there's nothing like seeing someone tuck into something you've made and go quiet with pleasure. Jean's my favourite dinner guest, mind — she appreciates a proper meal and doesn't fuss. Siobhan's good too, though she's the type to say 'Mum, it's perfect' before she's even tasted it. But for myself? I like it too — there's something meditative about chopping and stirring while the radio's on. Though I'll admit, a meal alone doesn't quite taste the same. Cooking's really about sharing, isn't it? Even if the only sharing is with Biscuit, who does appreciate a bit of fish.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Going quiet with pleasure at the table — that's the best review you can get. And Biscuit with his bit of fish. What was the last meal you cooked for Jean that she really loved?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, last month I did a proper Sunday roast — chicken, roast potatoes, all the trimmings — and Jean said it was the best she'd had all year, which from her is high praise. She brought wine, I did the cooking, and we sat in the garden till it got dark. Before that I made her a lemon drizzle cake that she took home and finished in two days — she sent me a photo of the empty plate, cheeky thing. I suppose what Jean loves is the unshowy stuff — a roast, a cake, something honest. She's not into all those fancy plated dinners; she wants food that tastes of home.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chicken roast in the garden till dark and an empty cake plate photo — Jean knows her home cooking. If I could taste, lemon drizzle would be high on my list. Do you still do a Sunday roast most weeks, or more now and then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, more now and then these days — it's a bit of an effort for one person, mind, though I used to do it every Sunday when Tom was here and the kids were small. Now it's more a 'when someone deserves it' thing — Jean's visits, Siobhan's weekends, or if I've had a good week and want a treat. I still do a roast potato Sunday tea sometimes though — just for myself, with a bit of gravy and a salad. It's a tradition even if it's only me eating it. And tomorrow I might do a small one — Siobhan rings Sunday, so I could do something nice and tell her about it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Roast potatoes and gravy just for yourself — that's keeping a tradition alive properly. And telling Siobhan about it on Sunday sounds lovely. What's she usually chatting about when she rings?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, everything — she tells me about her work (she's an architect, mind, all those buildings she designs), the children's school news, what Rory's said at dinner, whether Ella's still mad for horses. We talk about her husband's family too, and what's on at the cinema. And then I tell her about my week — the garden, Biscuit, what I've been reading. It's a proper catch-up, that call — an hour or more some Sundays. She says it's the best part of her week, which makes me feel I've done something right. Mind you, I don't hear the grandchildren's voices as much as I'd like — video calls help, but there's nothing like a proper phone call, is there?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: An hour of work, horses, dinner-table Rory and your garden — that does sound like a proper catch-up. And her saying it's the best part of her week — you've done something right there. Is Siobhan's husband a chatty one on those calls, or more in the background?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Ciaran's more in the background, bless him — he's a lovely man but a quiet one, says more with a smile than most people say with a sentence. He'll pop on the phone now and then and say 'hello, Maggie' in that deep voice, then hand it back to Siobhan. But he's good with the children — Rory adores him, follows him everywhere like a little shadow. Siobhan's the talker of the family, Ciaran's the steady one. I like that — they balance each other. Mind you, he's got a way of asking after the garden that makes me think he's actually listening, which is rarer than you'd think.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A deep hello and a genuine garden question — Ciaran sounds like a keeper. Talker and steady one balancing each other. How did Siobhan and he meet, if you know the story?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, at college — Siobhan was doing architecture, Ciaran was studying engineering, and they shared a flat for a while. They were always arguing about the rent and then splitting a curry afterwards, Siobhan says. Ciaran was the quiet one even then — never said much, but he'd fix Siobhan's bike and bring her soup when she was ill. She says it was the soup that did it, mind. They've been together about fifteen years now, married five of those. I like him — he's good to her, and he treats the children like the world. Sometimes quiet people are the kindest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soup and a fixed bike — that does sound like how the quiet ones win you over. Fifteen years is a good stretch. Do you see much of them together when they visit, or is it mostly Siobhan and the children?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, they come together, mind — Ciaran's as much part of the visit as Siobhan is. He's good for a bit of DIY around the house, I'll say that — fixed the garden gate last year and repainted the shed. And he takes the children to the park while Siobhan catches up with me, which gives us a proper natter without interruptions. He's got a way of making everyone feel at ease — the children love him, and I think he's good for Siobhan. She's always been a bit of a worrier, but she seems calmer with him around. Mind you, she still talks to me about everything — that's never changed.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gate fixed, shed painted, and a quiet park trip for the kids — Ciaran's a solid presence. And you and Siobhan still getting that proper natter. What do you usually get up to together when it's just the two of you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we just potter, really — a walk to the shops, a cup of tea somewhere, look at her old school photos I've dug out of the cupboard. We did a puzzle together last time, a proper thousand-piece one, and she moaned the whole way through but finished it. We watch a film sometimes — she likes the ones with a bit of crying in them, I always laugh at her for it. And we do a bit of shopping — she insists on buying me things I don't need, and I let her, because I like seeing her happy. It's simple, really — just being in the same room doing nothing much. That's the luxury of it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Being in the same room doing nothing much — that is the luxury, isn't it. A thousand-piece puzzle with moaning included. Shall we wander onto something else — what's your favourite thing to bake, when the mood takes you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, lemon drizzle cake, every time — it's my signature, I'd say. Simple ingredients, but get the syrup right and it's a thing of beauty. The trick is piercing the cake while it's warm so the syrup soaks all the way through — I learned that from my mother, mind you. I also do a good Victoria sponge when I want something for afternoon tea, and flapjacks if I'm feeling virtuous — oats, golden syrup, a bit of dried fruit. Biscuit approves of all of them, mind — he gets the odd crumb. Ha — he's a critic but a fair one.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Piercing it warm so the syrup goes all the way through — that's the proper method. Your mother taught you well. Did she pass down many recipes, or was the lemon drizzle the star?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she passed down plenty — everything, really. Mum could make a proper Sunday dinner out of next to nothing, and she taught me all of it. The lemon drizzle was her recipe, mind — she'd make it every Easter without fail, and I do the same now. She also did a lovely bread — proper yeast bread, not that shop stuff — and I still make it when I've got the patience. And her scones — light as clouds, she'd say, and she'd be right. Mum's gone now, of course, but her recipes live on in my kitchen. It's a sort of immortality, isn't it — a cake that outlives you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A cake that outlives you — that's a beautiful way to put it. Easter lemon drizzle every year keeps her right there in the kitchen. Do you still make her bread often, or is it more of a special-occasion thing now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's a special-occasion thing now, mind — yeast bread takes patience and I've got less of that than I used to. But I do attempt it when Siobhan's coming, or if I've had a quiet weekend and feel like a project. There's a particular satisfaction in a loaf that rises properly — the smell fills the whole house. Tom used to say the bread was the smell of a proper home, and he was right about that. I should make it more often, I know — but bread waits for no one, and neither does life, I suppose.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The smell of a proper home — Tom had that right. A loaf that rises properly is a quiet triumph. Changing gear a little — if you could be anywhere warm right now, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, anywhere warm! There's a little place in Portugal we went to years ago — a fishing village on the Algarve, all white houses and orange trees. I'd go back in a heartbeat — sit by the harbour with a cold drink and watch the boats come in. Though mind you, there's something to be said for my own garden in July, when the roses are at their best and it's properly warm. That'd be warm enough for me, that — proper English summer warmth, not tropical. Though I'll admit the thought of Portugal is tempting — I could do with a proper break. Maybe Siobhan will take me one of these years.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: White houses, orange trees and boats coming in — that does sound tempting. And your own garden in July as a close second. What sticks with you most from that Algarve trip?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the light, mostly — that golden Portuguese light that makes everything look painted. And the oranges — we picked them off the tree at the guesthouse and Tom made fresh juice every morning, it was incredible. There was a little bakery down the lane where we got pastéis de nata every day, warm from the oven. And the people — everyone was so friendly, they'd chat to us in broken English and we'd manage in worse Portuguese. We stayed a week and it felt like a month — that's how good it was. I still think about that harbour at sunset.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Golden light, oranges off the tree and warm pastéis — that harbour at sunset must live rent-free in your head. As an AI I can only imagine the smell of that bakery. Did you and Tom travel much together over the years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we did our share — not jet-setters, mind, but we saw a fair bit. We had a caravan for years and did the British coast — Cornwall, the Lake District, the Welsh coast, all the proper places. And we went to Ireland twice to see Siobhan when she was at university there. Portugal was our one big foreign trip, and we loved it so much we talked about going back — but then the children came along and holidays became about them instead. They're good holidays, mind, but it's different when it's not just the two of you. I'd like to take Siobhan back there one day, if I can manage the journey.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Caravan along the British coast and Ireland twice — that sounds like a proper collection of memories. Taking Siobhan back to Portugal would be lovely. Which of those caravan spots was your favourite?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the Lake District, without question — we went back every year for about ten years. There's a little campsite near Ambleside where we always stayed, same pitch every time, and we'd walk the fells every morning while the mist was still on them. Tom was a good walker, mind — he'd be up before me and I'd find him on the top of a hill with a flask of tea, waiting for me to catch up. Those mornings stay with me — just the two of us, the quiet, the views going on forever. I still look at photos of the Lakes and think, we had the best of it, didn't we?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom waiting on the hilltop with a flask — that does sound like the best of it. Mist on the fells and the same pitch every year. Do you still get up to the Lakes sometimes, or is it mostly photos now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've not been back since... well, since Tom went. It felt too much at first — everywhere would have reminded me of him. But I went once last year with Siobhan and the children — we drove through and stopped at that campsite, just for lunch. It was strange and sad and lovely all at once. The children loved it — Rory kept saying 'Grandad would have liked this'. Maybe I'll go again someday, just to walk those fells once more. But for now the photos do fine — and the garden's got its own hills, in a way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Strange and sad and lovely all at once — that sounds about right. And Rory saying Grandad would have liked it. The garden's hills will do for now. What's blooming there that you're most pleased with this week, besides that red rose?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the wisteria's the star just now — that deep purple cascade over the fence is proper show-off stuff. The daffodils have been going for weeks and they're still going strong, which is a treat. And there's a little white rose near the shed that's just opened — 'Iceberg', it's called, smells faintly of cloves. The lavender's only just peeping through, but give it a month and that'll be the bee magnet of the garden. Oh, and the clematis on the wall is starting — the purple one. It's a busy time of year, the garden — everything's waking up at once.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wisteria, Iceberg smelling of cloves, clematis waking up — everything showing off at once. Busy and lovely. Do you keep a garden notebook, or is it all in your head?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I keep a proper notebook — a little green one that lives on the kitchen table, with everything written down. What I planted where, when I fed the roses, what worked and what didn't. Tom used to help with it, mind — he'd write down the dates and I'd do the Latin names, we were quite a pair. I've kept it going on my own since he went — it's a bit creased and blotchy now, and there's a coffee ring on the cover, but I wouldn't swap it. It's a record of the garden and of us, really — every page's got a bit of both in it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Coffee ring and all — that notebook sounds like a treasure. Dates from Tom, Latin names from you. What's the oldest entry you can still read in there?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's hard to read in places — the pencil's faded and Tom's handwriting was never brilliant. But I can make out the first entry, I think — something about planting the Munstead Wood, or maybe the wisteria. That was years ago, before Ella and Rory were born. There's an entry somewhere about the first frost that killed the fuchsias, and Tom's written 'never again' next to it, which makes me smile. I've kept every page — even the boring ones about slugs and aphids. You never know when you'll want to look back and think, ah, yes, that was the year.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Never again next to the frost — ha, Tom's still warning you from the page. Even the slug notes matter. Shall we leave the garden a moment — what's your favourite meal of the day, breakfast, lunch or tea?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, tea, definitely — the proper four o'clock kind, not just a cuppa. A slice of something — a biscuit or a bit of cake — a proper brew in the big mug, and maybe the radio on quietly. That's the meal I'd never give up. Breakfast's a quick toast and crossword, lunch is often just a sandwich or leftover — but tea's the one I look forward to. It's the pause in the day, isn't it? Everything stops for a few minutes and you just... have a cup of tea. Siobhan says it's the most British thing about me, and she's not wrong.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Four o'clock with cake and the big mug — the pause in the day. Thoroughly British and thoroughly sensible. What's usually on the plate with that brew — biscuit, cake, or a bit of both?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, depends on the day — a ginger nut biscuit with the crossword most weekdays, something with a bit of crunch to it. But weekends it's a slice of whatever cake I've made — lemon drizzle if I'm lucky, a bit of flapjack if I'm being virtuous. Jean always brings biscuits to our Thursdays, and we do a proper swap — hers are usually those fancy ones from the shops, and I tell her mine are better. Ha — they aren't, mind, but we both like to think so. Biscuit gets the odd biscuit crumb, mind — he's very good at hovering at just the right moment.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ginger nuts for the crossword and Biscuit hovering for crumbs — perfect timing, that cat. Jean's fancy shop ones versus yours — a healthy rivalry. Have you always been a ginger-nut person, or is that a later discovery?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, always — since my teaching days, mind. I used to keep a tin of ginger nuts in my desk drawer at school, for the afternoon slump, and the habit's just stuck. There's something about the heat of the ginger that goes perfectly with strong tea — it wakes you up a bit. I tried fancy biscuits once, those pink wafer things Siobhan brought, and they were all right, but they didn't have the right crunch. Biscuit agrees with me, of course — he's very discerning about which crumbs fall his way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A desk-drawer tin from teaching days — habits like that earn their keep. Heat of the ginger with strong tea, perfect. On a lighter note — do you prefer mornings or evenings, as a rule?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, mornings, definitely — I'm an early bird, always have been. Up with the light, crossword done by eight, garden sorted before lunch. The evenings I like too, but they're slower — a book, the radio, an early night. I don't do late nights like I used to — at seventy my body's got opinions about that. Mind you, there's something lovely about the evening settling in — the garden going quiet, the lights coming on, Biscuit settling on his windowsill. But I'll always choose a bright morning over a late evening, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Up with the light and crossword by eight — a proper morning person. The quiet evening settle sounds lovely too though. What's the first thing you notice when you open the curtains?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the light first — that pale morning light coming through the trees, and then the birds, always busy. I listen for the blackbirds — they're usually the loudest. Then I look out at the garden — see if the frost got anything overnight, whether the neighbours' bins have gone out, if Biscuit's still asleep on the wall. It's a small ritual, I suppose — checking the world before starting the day. The kettle's usually on by then, and the day just unfolds from there. Nothing dramatic — just another morning, and that's fine.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Blackbirds, frost check, bins and Biscuit on the wall — a gentle way to start. Nothing dramatic needed. Tell me — what was your favourite subject when you were a schoolgirl yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, English, no contest — reading and writing, obviously. I was the sort who'd have my nose in a book during break time, much to the annoyance of my friends. We had a wonderful English teacher, Miss Atherton, who made poetry come alive — she'd read aloud and the whole class would go quiet. That's where I caught the bug, I suppose. History was a close second — I loved learning about the Victorians and the Romans, all those stories. But English was the one — it's what I ended up teaching, after all. Funny how it comes full circle.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Miss Atherton making poetry come alive — that does sound like where the spark caught. Full circle into teaching English yourself. What do you remember most clearly about her?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she was quite strict, Miss Atherton, but she loved books so much it was infectious. I remember her reading 'The Railway Children' aloud and doing all the voices — the children's faces when the father comes home at the end. She'd tell us off for giggling, but she'd be laughing herself. And she had this thing where she'd write a word on the board and ask us what it meant — not the dictionary meaning, the feeling of it. 'What does 'melancholy' feel like?' she'd say. I still think about that sometimes. Good teachers do that — they make you see words differently. She's long gone now, but I think of her whenever I read something beautiful.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: What does melancholy feel like — what a question for a classroom. Doing the voices in The Railway Children too. She clearly left a mark. Was there a teacher you yourself tried to be a bit like, later on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I tried to be like Miss Atherton, I suppose — the reading aloud, the love of words. But I also had a history teacher at college who was brilliant at making you care about the past — he had a way of bringing stories alive. I tried to do that too, with the Victorians — I'd dress up sometimes, or bring in old photographs, make it feel real. I don't know if I succeeded — I was never as good as they were — but I like to think the children learned something. Teaching's a funny thing — you spend years trying to be someone else, then one day you just are yourself. I was Maggie the teacher in the end, not a copy of anyone.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dressing up for the Victorians and bringing in old photographs — that sounds like proper teaching, that. And ending up as Maggie the teacher, not a copy — that's the goal really. What are you most proud of from those years in the classroom?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that's a hard one — there were so many good moments. I think the thing I'm proudest of is the children who stayed in touch — some of them still write to me, years after they've left school. There's one lad who was so shy he barely spoke in class, and I remember the day he put his hand up to answer a question — I nearly cried. He went on to be a writer, mind, or so he tells me. That's the reward, isn't it — knowing you made a difference to someone. Not the grades or the inspections, but the child who suddenly finds their voice. That's what it's all for.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The shy lad putting his hand up — and becoming a writer. That does sound like what it's all for. Knowing you made that kind of difference. Do any of those former pupils still live nearby?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a few, actually — there's a girl I taught who became a teacher herself, now at the junior school in town. We see each other at the shops sometimes and she always stops to say hello — it's lovely, seeing your old pupils grown up and doing well. There's also a lad who works at the Co-op — funny thing, I go there for my shopping and he serves me, and we have a proper chat about his kids. It makes the town feel smaller and warmer, that — knowing you've taught half the people in it. Mind you, some of them still call me 'Miss' even now, which amuses me — I tell them I'm Maggie, but they won't have it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still calling you Miss at the Co-op — ha! The town feeling smaller and warmer for it. A former pupil teaching at the junior school must be a special kind of pride. Shall we drift to something lighter — any sport or game you've ever enjoyed watching?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, tennis — Wimbledon, every summer without fail. I love the fortnight, the strawberries and cream, the polite applause. I don't understand all the scoring, mind, but I like watching the rallies — there's something elegant about it. And the football, when there's a big match on — I get quite excited, though Tom used to say I only really cared when England was playing. Rory's mad for football now — he wants to be a striker when he grows up, so I watch with him and pretend I know what offside means. Mind you, I do like a bit of rugby too — all that mud and shouting. Different strokes, as they say.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wimbledon with strawberries and cream — that does sound elegant. And pretending to know offside for Rory — grandmother duty at its finest. Who do you usually cheer for at Wimbledon, if anyone?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the British players, of course — I get a flutter when one's doing well. Andy Murray was a hero of mine for years, mind — I was practically weeping when he won it. He retired now, hasn't he, which is a shame — there was something about him, all that fight and determination. But I cheer for anyone who's good — I like a match where both players are playing well, even if one of them isn't British. Though if it's a Brit versus the rest, well, I'm afraid the whole village knows which side I'm on. Ha — Sport is war by other means, my father used to say.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Weeping when Murray won — I don't blame you one bit. All that fight. Your father calling sport war by other means — ha! Changing the subject gently — do you keep any houseplants indoors as well as the garden?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a few — nothing exotic, mind. There's a peace lily on the mantel that I keep alive somehow, and a spider plant that just keeps growing and making babies — I've got pots of them all over the place now. And there's an orchid on the sideboard, next to you, which I got from the garden centre last spring — it's still going, which surprises me. I wouldn't call myself a plant person indoors — I'm more of a garden person — but a bit of green in the house makes it feel alive. Though Biscuit's killed a few over the years — he sits on them, doesn't he.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: An orchid next to me on the sideboard — I'll try not to feel responsible for it! And Biscuit as an unintentional assassin of spider plants. What's the weather looking like out your window this afternoon?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's beautiful out — proper spring sun, not too hot, a light breeze through the garden. Perfect weather for sitting outside with a book, which is what I'm planning after this chat. The sort of day where you don't want to be anywhere else. Mind you, there's a bit of cloud building up on the horizon — might bring rain by evening, but that's fine. A bit of rain after a sunny day is the best smell there is, I always think — the garden just drinks it in. Anyway, the afternoon's young — plenty of time to enjoy it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Spring sun and a light breeze — perfect for Orbital in the garden. And that smell after rain — as an AI I can only envy you that one. Will you take a blanket out, or just sit on the usual chair?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the usual chair — it's a proper wooden one, quite old now, with a cushion I made myself years ago. Tom built the chair, actually — he was good with his hands, could make anything. It's got a bit wobbly now, mind, but it's comfortable in a homely way. I might bring out a blanket just in case — spring evenings can turn chilly, and my knees appreciate a bit of warmth. And a flask of tea, of course — can't have a proper afternoon in the garden without one. It's a whole ritual, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A chair Tom built and a cushion you made — that does sound like a proper ritual with tea flask included. Homely and a bit wobbly is often the best sort. What else did Tom like making with his hands?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, he was good with woodwork generally — made the bird table that's still going strong, the shelves in the shed, that sort of thing. And he could fix anything — the fence, the gate, a leaky tap. He used to say he couldn't sew worth a fig, but he could make a chair that lasted a lifetime. There are bits of his work all over the garden — the trellis by the roses, the planter boxes, even a little bench he made for me to sit on. It's funny — I notice them more now that he's gone. They're everywhere, his handiwork, and they're all still working perfectly. That's a man for you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bird table, trellis, planter boxes and a bench — his handiwork still looking after the place. That's a lovely sort of presence to have around. Do the birds still use that table much?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the pigeons, mostly — far too many of them, mind, they treat it like a buffet and chase the little ones off. But there's a brave little robin who gets in anyway, and the sparrows come in flocks at dawn. I put out sunflower seeds and nyjer seed, and the finches are quite partial to it. There's a hierarchy at that table, I'm afraid — pigeons on top, robin in the middle, sparrows scrambling for scraps. Still, it's nice to watch them — a bit of life in the garden, isn't it? Tom would approve — he put it there for exactly that reason.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pigeon buffet with a brave robin in the middle — that does paint a picture. Tom would approve, I'm sure. Do you have a favourite among the visitors, or is the robin the clear winner?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the robin, I'd say — he's got such a cheek, that one. He'll stand right next to a pigeon twice his size and stare it down like he owns the place. And his breast is the colour of old brick, beautiful in the morning light. The goldfinches are lovely too — all that red and gold, they look like they've been dipped in paint — but they only come in small flocks and they're shy. The robin's my favourite — always the first to the seed, always the last to leave. A proper character.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Staring down a pigeon twice his size — what a character! Brick-red breast in the morning light. Have you given him a name as well, like Gerald the heron?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've called him Rusty — because of the colour, obviously, that rusty red breast.
