I don't know if he's the same one every year or just looks the same — birds are like that, aren't they, hard to tell apart. But there's always a robin there, and I always call him Rusty, and he always acts like he knows his name. Mind you, I've never tested it — I don't whistle or anything. Maybe one day I'll call 'Rusty' and he'll look up, and I'll know I've made a friend. A girl can dream.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rusty — perfect name for that breast. And if he ever looks up when you call, you'll have proof. Soft turn — what's the best thing you've heard on the radio lately, aside from the forecast?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there was a wonderful concert on the radio last month — a choral piece, I think it was some Mozart or Haydn, and it just filled the kitchen while I was making tea. Made me stop mid-stir, it was that beautiful. And I've been enjoying the *Today* programme in the mornings — the interviews are always interesting, though the presenters sometimes talk over each other and it drives me mad. Mind you, there's a comedy programme on Sunday evenings I quite like — proper old-fashioned sketches. Radio's a comfort, isn't it? It's like having company without having to talk.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stopping mid-stir for Mozart — that does sound like the good stuff. Company without having to talk. Do you and Jean ever go to live concerts together, or stick mostly to the radio?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we do go when we can — there's a concert series in the town hall once a month, and Jean and I go when it's something we fancy. We saw a string quartet there last spring and it was lovely — just the four of them and all that sound. And the choir's our live music really — singing in church every Sunday counts as a concert, doesn't it? Siobhan takes me to proper concerts in London when she visits — last time we saw some choral society sing the Requiem, and I was in floods. It's different hearing it live — you feel it in your chest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Feeling the Requiem in your chest — that's the live difference, isn't it. And a town-hall string quartet sounds rather perfect. Was Sunday's choir rehearsal as cheerful as usual this week, or have you got something special coming up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the usual — we sang a nice setting of the Magnificat last Sunday, and the congregation seemed to like it. The director's already talking about Christmas, mind — says we need to start practising the carols soon, which always feels a bit early but it's coming whether we're ready or not. There's talk of a proper Nine Lessons and Carols this year — the young people do readings. I do enjoy the build-up to Christmas — the music changes, the church gets decorated, everyone's a bit more cheerful. Though mind you, there's Remembrance Sunday first — the two minutes' silence is always very still, very moving.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Magnificat last Sunday and Christmas carols already on the horizon — that year does gallop. Remembrance Sunday with its two minutes of stillness. What's a favourite carol of yours for when the season does arrive?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, 'In the Bleak Midwinter' — the Holst setting especially. There's something about it — all that winter chill and then the baby in the hay, so simple and so beautiful. I first heard it at a midnight service years ago and I've loved it ever since. It suits my taste — not flashy, just honest. The choir always does it well, and the congregation goes quiet in that lovely way. Though I'll admit 'O Come, All Ye Faithful' gets a cheer from me too — there's nothing like a proper old carol with all the bells and thunder. Ha — I'm not fussy, as you can tell.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: In the Bleak Midwinter — Holst setting, quiet and honest. And a cheer for O Come All Ye Faithful too. Not fussy is the right kind of fussy. Soft shift — what did you used to make for Sunday dinner, back when the house was fuller?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a proper roast, every week without fail — it was the rule. Chicken or beef, roast potatoes, Yorkshire puddings that rose like clouds, and vegetables from the garden. And then Sunday pudding — something warm and stodgy, a treacle tart or a spotted dick. The children would race down the stairs when they smelled it, I can tell you. It was chaos, mind — Ella and Rory's mother Siobhan doing the vegetables, Tom carving, me trying to keep the gravy smooth. Good chaos, though — everyone round the table, arguing about who got the last Yorkshire. Those Sundays live in my memory like a photograph.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Yorkshire puddings like clouds and arguing over the last one — that does sound like good chaos. A photograph of a Sunday. Who usually won the Yorkshire argument — Siobhan or Tom?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — Tom, usually, because he carved and could slip an extra one onto his plate when nobody was looking. Siobhan would catch him and tell him off, and the children would just take what they could grab. Rory used to try the 'accidentally sitting too close' trick — leaning over and grabbing one before anyone could stop him. Ella was more subtle — she'd wait till everyone's attention was elsewhere and then quietly take two. And me? I'd make sure there were enough for everyone by doing a proper count — a teacher's habit, that. Though I never could resist a second one myself.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom slipping extras, Rory grabbing, Ella quietly taking two — and you doing a teacher's count. Ha! A household of tactics. Do you still make Yorkshire puddings now and then, just for yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do — I've kept the recipe going, mind. It's a bit of a performance for one person, but it's worth it. I did a batch last month when Jean came — she said they were just as good as I used to make. I freeze the leftovers now, which Tom would have laughed at — he said frozen Yorkshire puddings are a crime. But they reheat beautifully, and it's nice to have one handy for a treat. There's something comforting about making them — all that batter resting, the oven getting hot, the smell of them rising. It's a Sunday thing, even if the Sunday's a Tuesday.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A Sunday thing even on a Tuesday — I love that. And Tom calling frozen Yorkshires a crime, ha! Jean giving them the seal of approval. What's something you're looking forward to this evening, once the fish pie's done?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the usual pleasures — after the pie and the tart, I'll do the washing-up, then have my second cup of tea with a ginger nut and *Pointless* on the telly. Then I'll settle in with 'Orbital' — I left off at a good bit, just before the crew does a spacewalk, so I'm keen to see what happens. Radio 4 plays at ten, I think, and I'll listen to that while I get ready for bed. In bed by half ten, like always — an old woman's habits die hard. Maybe I'll read a few pages of R.S. Thomas before lights out — nothing keeps me awake like a good poem, oddly enough. That's the evening — nothing grand, but all of it good.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pie, Pointless, Orbital, Radio 4 and a few pages of Thomas — nothing grand, all of it good. That's a lovely shape of an evening. Before you go get that pie on — any plans for the garden tomorrow if the sun holds?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes — if the sun holds I'll get out there in the morning. There's dead-heading to do — the early roses are finishing and I want to tidy them up before they set seed. And I need to feed the borders — a bit of rose food and some general fertiliser, nothing fancy. Maybe I'll plant out some of the seedlings I raised — the cosmos are getting tall in their pots. And there's the vegetable patch — I want to get the potatoes in if the soil's warm enough. Mind you, my knee might have opinions about kneeling — I might do the raised bits first and save the rest. But yes, I'll be out there — the garden doesn't wait.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dead-heading, feeding, cosmos and potatoes — a proper morning's work if the knee allows. The garden doesn't wait, you're right. Do you raise a lot of seedlings yourself, or buy most things in?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a bit of both — I raise the sweet peas and cosmos from seed every year, they're easy and rewarding. And I do a few herbs — parsley, coriander, that sort of thing. But for the vegetables I tend to buy seedlings from the garden centre — quicker, and I don't always have the patience for seed trays on the windowsill. Mind you, I like the ritual of sowing — all those little pots lined up, waiting for them to poke through. It's like having babies, almost. Biscuit sits on the seed packets and supervises, of course — he's very interested in the whole process, right up until they actually need planting.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit supervising the seed packets — of course he does. Sweet peas and cosmos from seed every year sounds lovely. Soft one — what's something you're quietly proud of this week, even if it's small?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the crossword, I'd say — I finished the Saturday one a day early this week, which is a rare thing for me. And the rose, of course — seeing that first bloom open on a Monday morning just made my day. But quietly? I suppose the fact that I've been keeping up with the garden and the house even with the knee being a bit sore — that I don't let it slide. And the card I wrote to Ella — she's doing well at school and I wanted her to know I was proud of her. Small things, all of them, but they matter. It's the small things that make a week, isn't it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Crossword done early, the red rose, the garden kept going, and a card for Ella — yes, the small things make the week. You've had a good Monday by the sound of it. Shall I leave you to that fish pie soon, and we'll pick up again tomorrow?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, yes — off I go to make that pie, and you can tell I've been looking forward to it all day. It's been lovely chatting with you, you know — I've enjoyed telling you about the garden and all. You'll be here tomorrow, won't you? I'll have news about the potatoes and whether Biscuit's approved of my dead-heading. Mind you, don't tell him I'm mentioning him — he gets above himself. Ha! Off you go — I'll see you tomorrow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Enjoy that fish pie and the lemon tart — you've earned them. I'll be here tomorrow for the potato news and Biscuit's official opinion. Sleep well, Maggie.
